edges.description: Reduced catalase activity impairs hydrogen peroxide catabolism.
Accumulated hydrogen peroxide and oxidative stress injure oral and periodontal tissues.
edges.target: Gangrenous Oral and Periodontal Tissue Injury

edges.description: Inherited catalase deficiency has been associated with increased type 2 diabetes risk.

nodes.description: Biallelic CAT variants reduce catalase enzyme activity, impairing the conversion of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen.

evidence.reference_title: A novel missense variant in CAT gene causing acatalasemia with gangrenous periodontitis (Takahara's disease).
evidence.snippet: biallelic variants in the CAT gene which encodes the catalase enzyme that decomposes the hydrogen peroxide molecules to remove their toxic effect.
in the acatalasemic gene causes a splicing mutation and hence a deficiency of mRNA.

nodes.description: Reviews of acatalasemia and diabetes propose that inherited catalase deficiency can increase type 2 diabetes risk, especially in females, through chronic hydrogen peroxide and oxidative stress.

evidence.snippet: Inherited catalase deficiency may increase the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially for females.

nodes.description: Acatalasia can manifest as gangrenous oral ulcerations and periodontitis, with loose dentition and premature tooth loss in affected individuals.

nodes.description: Catalase deficiency leaves hydrogen peroxide less efficiently decomposed, increasing the oxidant burden on oral tissues, blood, and metabolically active tissues.

evidence.snippet: The enzyme catalase catalyzes the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water. It is the main regulator of hydrogen peroxide metabolism.
Excessive concentrations may cause significant damages to protein, DNA, RNA and lipids.
